title: Rival Wives and Faithful Increase
summary: Through a rivalry of wives, handmaids, and mandrakes God builds Jacob’s family, remembers Rachel with Joseph, and multiplies Jacob’s flocks despite Laban’s fraud.
historicalContext: Jacob is still in Paddan-aram, serving Laban near Haran in upper Mesopotamia. Fourteen years of labour have bought him two wives, and the second half of that term overlaps with the births recorded here. The customs in view belong to the patriarchal world: a barren wife could give her maid to her husband so that the child would be counted as hers, a practice known from Mesopotamian legal texts and already tried by Sarah with Hagar. Children secured a woman’s standing, and barrenness was felt as public disgrace. Pastoral life shaped wages: a herdsman was commonly paid with a share of the flock’s increase, and in that region sheep were normally white and goats dark, so multicoloured animals were the exception. Laban’s household also practised divination and kept household gods, which shows how much pagan thinking surrounded the family through whom God was keeping His promise.
literaryContext: Genesis 30 continues the birth narrative that began at 29:31, where the LORD saw that Leah was unloved and opened her womb. The section is arranged as a contest: Rachel answers Leah through Bilhah, Leah answers through Zilpah, the mandrakes become a bargaining token, and the scene closes when God remembers Rachel and gives Joseph. Each name is explained by a short speech that lets the reader hear the mothers’ hearts. The key word “hire” or “wages” links the marriage bargain of chapter 29, the mandrake deal, and the flock contract that fills the second half of the chapter. The contest then moves from the tent to the pasture as Jacob and Laban trade schemes over speckled and spotted animals. Chapter 31 must be read alongside these verses, for there Jacob learns and confesses that his increase came from God, who saw Laban’s wrongs and kept the Bethel promise of 28:15.
themes: God builds His people through flawed families
Envy, rivalry, and the misuse of human expedients
The Giver of life versus superstition
God remembers and hears the despised
Faithful labour under an unjust master
Promised blessing that no scheme can block

outline.title: Rachel’s Envy and Bilhah’s Sons
outline.summary: Barren Rachel demands children, gives her maid to Jacob, and names Dan and Naphtali as signs of vindication and victory over her sister.

outline.title: Leah Answers Through Zilpah
outline.summary: When Leah stops bearing, she follows Rachel’s method and names Zilpah’s sons Gad and Asher with words of fortune and happiness.

outline.summary: Jacob uses rods and selective breeding, but the increase that makes him exceedingly rich is God’s doing, as chapter 31 makes plain.

verses.bibleText: And when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister; and said unto Jacob, Give me children, or else I die.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene opens with Rachel watching. Leah has borne four sons in succession (29:32–35), and every birth has reminded Rachel of her own empty arms. The narrator says plainly that “Rachel envied her sister.” The verb describes jealousy that burns against another person’s good, the same passion that would later drive Joseph’s brothers (37:11). Envy is never content with grief over its own loss; it wants the rival brought low. Rachel held Jacob’s love, yet that did not satisfy her while her sister held the honour of motherhood.

Her words to Jacob are sharp: “Give me children, or else I die.” In the ancient world a barren wife lived under a cloud of shame, and Rachel’s distress is understandable. Yet her demand is aimed at the wrong person and in the wrong spirit. Sarah had waited decades for Isaac, and Rebekah had waited twenty years until Isaac prayed (25:21). Rachel, comparing herself with a fertile sister, could not wait even a few years. The phrase “or else I die” is the language of despair, as though life without a son was no life at all.

The narrator’s wording also places Rachel’s envy alongside Leah’s pain. The previous chapter ended with the LORD seeing that Leah was hated (29:31); this one begins with Rachel seeing that she bore no children. Each sister looked at the other and saw only what she lacked. Leah longed for the love Rachel had, and Rachel longed for the sons Leah had. Neither could enjoy her own portion, because both measured it against her sister’s.

There is a painful irony in her cry. Rachel would one day bear a second son, and in that childbirth she would die (35:16–19). What she demanded as the cure for her sorrow became the occasion of her death. Scripture does not mock her pain, but it shows how desires, even good ones, become destructive when they are turned into the condition for living.

Hannah, who also suffered under a fruitful rival, offers the contrast (1 Samuel 1:6–11). She too wept and would not eat, but she carried her anguish into the house of the LORD and poured out her soul before Him. Rachel carried hers to Jacob. The difference points every troubled heart to the One who alone can answer such a longing and who satisfies the soul even when the longing remains.

wordNotes.term: וַתְּקַנֵּא (vattekanne) — envied
wordNotes.explanation: The verb qanaʾ expresses intense, possessive zeal. Directed toward God it can describe His rightful jealousy for His covenant people; directed toward a neighbour it becomes envy that resents another’s good. Here Rachel’s zeal is turned against her own sister, and the same verb later describes the brothers’ resentment of Joseph, showing how the passion passed down the family.

wordNotes.term: הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים (havah-li vanim) — give me children
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative havah is an urgent “give!” Rachel speaks to Jacob as though he controlled the womb. The demand sets up Jacob’s reply in the next verse and the narrator’s later insistence that God is the one who gives and withholds children.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel: and he said, Am I in God's stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob answers heat with heat: “Jacob’s anger was kindled against Rachel.” His question, “Am I in God’s stead, who hath withheld from thee the fruit of the womb?” is theologically correct. Life is God’s gift, and no husband can command conception. Rachel’s demand had placed on Jacob a burden only the Creator can bear, and he refused it.

Yet a true statement can be spoken in a wrong spirit. Jacob offers no sympathy, no shared sorrow, and no prayer. His own father had entreated the LORD for a barren wife, and the LORD had answered (25:21). Jacob had seen the God of Bethel and received the promise of a multiplied seed (28:14), but here he does not bring Rachel’s need before that God. He names God only to push the problem away from himself. The result is that the household turns from prayer to human contrivance in the very next verse. His silence before God stands in contrast with the faith he would later show at Peniel, where he refused to let go until he was blessed.

The household’s pattern of anger deserves notice. Rachel’s envy provokes Jacob’s wrath, and Jacob’s wrath drives Rachel to a scheme that will provoke Leah. Scripture warns that the wrath of man does not work the righteousness of God (James 1:20). Anger may be justified by the facts, yet it rarely brings healing. A soft answer might have opened a door to shared prayer; a hard one shut it.

The same question returns at the end of Genesis on the lips of Joseph, Rachel’s longed-for son. When his brothers fear revenge, Joseph says, “Am I in the place of God?” (50:19). There the words express humble trust that God has turned evil into good. Spoken by Jacob they close a conversation; spoken by Joseph they open the way to forgiveness. The family would learn over many years what it means to leave to God the things that belong to God.

Every believer who faces another’s grief can learn from Jacob’s failure. It is not enough to be right about God’s sovereignty. Love brings the sufferer to God in prayer and carries the weight together (Galatians 6:2).

wordNotes.term: הֲתַחַת אֱלֹהִים אָנֹכִי (hatachat ʾElohim ʾanokhi) — am I in God’s stead?
wordNotes.explanation: Tachat means “under” or “in place of.” The rhetorical question strongly denies that Jacob can do what only God does. The identical question in Joseph’s mouth (50:19) forms a bookend to the family story, and the Syrian king’s cry “Am I God, to kill and to make alive?” uses the same logic.

wordNotes.term: פְּרִי־בָטֶן (peri-vaten) — fruit of the womb
wordNotes.explanation: A common idiom for children, it presents offspring as fruit that grows from God’s blessing. The Law promises it as covenant blessing, and the Psalms call it His reward, so the phrase already points beyond Jacob to God.

verses.bibleText: And she said, Behold my maid Bilhah, go in unto her; and she shall bear upon my knees, that I may also have children by her.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rachel now takes matters into her own hands. “Behold my maid Bilhah, go in unto her.” Bilhah had been given to Rachel by Laban at the wedding (29:29), and under the customs of the day a barren wife could present her maid to her husband so that any child born would be legally hers. Mesopotamian contracts and law collections record the practice, and Abraham’s household had used it with Hagar (16:2). The very words echo Sarah’s: “that I may also have children by her” is literally “that I also may be built from her.”

The echo is a warning. Sarah’s plan had produced contempt, quarrels, and an exiled mother and son. Rachel had less excuse than Sarah, for Jacob already had four sons and there was no question of an heir. Her aim was not to preserve the promise but to match her sister. A custom being legal and common did not make it right before God, whose design for marriage was one man and one woman becoming one flesh (2:24).

“She shall bear upon my knees” describes a recognised act of adoption or legitimation. A child placed on the knees of a parent or grandparent was received as belonging to that person’s family. Jacob would later take Joseph’s sons from between his knees as his own (48:12), and Joseph would receive his great-grandchildren on his knees (50:23). Rachel intends to claim Bilhah’s child from the moment of birth. The custom gave Rachel legal standing, but it could not give her the joy of bearing her own child.

The verse shows how impatience can clothe itself in respectable custom. God would still overrule these choices, for the sons of the handmaids became tribes in Israel. But the narrative never forgets their cost. The divided household and the bitter rivalries that follow trace back to decisions like this one, made apart from prayer. Paul’s reflection on Sarah and Hagar shows how Scripture views such arrangements: the child born “after the flesh” stands in contrast to the child born by promise (Galatians 4:22–23).

wordNotes.term: עַל־בִּרְכַּי (ʿal-birkay) — upon my knees
wordNotes.explanation: Knees (berekh) in this setting signify formal acceptance of a child into one’s family line. Job’s lament about the knees that received him, and Joseph’s reception of Machir’s children, show the same gesture of welcome and belonging.

wordNotes.term: וְאִבָּנֶה (veʾibbaneh) — that I may have children (be built)
wordNotes.explanation: The verb banah means “to build.” It sounds like ben, “son,” and the wordplay presents children as the building of a house or family line. Sarah used the same expression with Hagar, and Ruth’s blessing later speaks of Rachel and Leah as the two who built the house of Israel.

verses.bibleText: And she gave him Bilhah her handmaid to wife: and Jacob went in unto her.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she gave him Bilhah her handmaid to wife: and Jacob went in unto her.” The narrator records the act without comment, but its brevity is telling. Jacob raises no objection and seeks no counsel from God. The same man who would one day wrestle until daybreak for a blessing here simply complies with his wife’s plan.

Bilhah is called a wife, though elsewhere she is named a concubine (35:22). In the patriarchal period the terms overlapped: such a woman was a secondary wife, subordinate to her mistress, with rights and children recognised in the household. Hagar and Keturah occupy a similar place. Jacob’s path thus moved from a marriage he did not choose to a polygamous home and then to concubinage. God would overrule these unions to form the tribes of Israel, but His overruling is not approval. The household’s later strife, including Reuben’s sin with Bilhah, shows what such arrangements bred. Even the patriarchs, who knew God’s promises, absorbed the marriage customs of their surroundings and paid for it in family sorrow. Jesus later pointed back past such concessions to the Creator’s design “from the beginning” (Matthew 19:8), showing that the patriarchal pattern was never the ideal.

Bilhah herself never speaks. She is given, she conceives, and she bears, while others name her children. Scripture’s silence about her voice is a reminder of how such customs treated women as instruments. The God who saw Hagar in the wilderness (16:13) also saw Bilhah, and her sons stand among the tribes whose names are written on the gates of the holy city (Revelation 21:12).

wordNotes.term: לְאִשָּׁה (leʾishshah) — to wife
wordNotes.explanation: ʾIshshah means woman or wife. Its use for Bilhah, who is also called pilegesh, “concubine,” shows that in the patriarchal era a handmaid given to the husband held the status of a secondary wife, distinct from a slave, yet beneath her mistress.

verses.bibleText: And Bilhah conceived, and bare Jacob a son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Bilhah conceived, and bare Jacob a son.” The sentence is plain, but the phrase “bare Jacob” matters. Whatever the rivalry between the sisters, each child is first of all Jacob’s son and so belongs to the line of promise. The covenant God had sworn that Jacob’s seed would be as the dust of the earth (28:14), and the narrative counts every birth toward that word.

The narrator does not say here that the LORD opened Bilhah’s womb, as he did for Leah (29:31). He leaves the theological explanation to Rachel in the next verse, inviting the reader to weigh her claim. Yet the child himself is real grace, and he would become the head of a tribe.

wordNotes.term: וַתֵּלֶד לְיַעֲקֹב בֵּן (vattéled leYaʿaqov ben) — bare Jacob a son
wordNotes.explanation: The preposition le, “to” or “for,” marks the child as Jacob’s. The same formula runs through the whole birth list, tying each son, whatever his mother, to the patriarch who carried the promise.

verses.bibleText: And Rachel said, God hath judged me, and hath also heard my voice, and hath given me a son: therefore called she his name Dan.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rachel interprets the birth: “God hath judged me, and hath also heard my voice, and hath given me a son: therefore called she his name Dan.” To be judged here means to be vindicated, to have one’s case decided in one’s favour. Rachel felt that her barrenness had been an injustice, set against Leah’s fruitfulness, and she reads Bilhah’s son as God’s verdict on her side.

Her words contain both faith and self-justification. She rightly confesses that God gives children and that He hears. “Heard my voice” may mean that she had prayed, or it may mean that she took the birth as God’s answer to her complaint in verse 1. Either way she credits God, which is better than crediting luck. Yet she also assumes that the success of her plan proves God approved it. The narrator, who says elsewhere that the LORD “saw” and “hearkened,” does not confirm her reading. Results do not automatically sanctify the methods that preceded them.

It is worth noticing how quickly Rachel moves from despair to triumph. In verse 1 she could not live without children; now, through a child not born from her own body, she speaks as one whose case has been settled in court. Her emotions rise and fall with her standing beside Leah. The psalmist who asked God to judge him did so while committing his way to the LORD and waiting for Him (Psalm 26:1). Rachel’s verdict was announced before the trial was over.

She uses the general name ʾElohim rather than the covenant name the LORD, which Leah had used for her own sons. The choice may hint at distance; Rachel speaks of God as Judge more than as the covenant Friend of the family. The tribe of Dan would later have a troubled history, turning early to idolatry (Judges 18:30), and Dan is missing from the list of sealed tribes in Revelation 7. A name that began as a claim of vindication became a reminder that only God’s judgment is final.

wordNotes.term: דָּנַנִּי (dananni) — hath judged me
wordNotes.explanation: From din, “to judge, plead a cause,” the verb here carries the sense of “vindicated me” or “given me justice.” The name Dan, “judge,” keeps the root. Jacob’s later blessing plays on the same word: “Dan shall judge his people.”

verses.bibleText: And Bilhah Rachel's maid conceived again, and bare Jacob a second son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Bilhah Rachel’s maid conceived again, and bare Jacob a second son.” The repetition of the arrangement suggests that Bilhah now had a settled place as Jacob’s secondary wife. The description “Rachel’s maid” keeps the rivalry in view: in the reckoning of the tent this child is Rachel’s second answer to Leah’s four.

The brevity lets the next verse carry the emotion. The plain record of conception and birth is itself a reminder that each new life was a gift woven into God’s promise to multiply Jacob’s seed.

wordNotes.term: שִׁפְחַת רָחֵל (shifchat Rachel) — Rachel’s maid
wordNotes.explanation: Shifchah denotes a female servant attached to her mistress personally, often given at marriage. The phrase underlines that Bilhah’s children were reckoned to Rachel, as Hagar’s son was to Sarah.

verses.bibleText: And Rachel said, With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed: and she called his name Naphtali.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
At Naphtali’s birth Rachel speaks openly of conflict: “With great wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and I have prevailed.” The words “great wrestlings” are literally “wrestlings of God.” The expression may simply be a superlative, meaning mighty struggles, but it may also mean that Rachel saw her contest with Leah as a struggle for God’s favour, a contest waged before God and about His blessing. Either way, she treats her sister as an opponent to be beaten.

The word “prevailed” is significant. It is the same verb the Angel uses when He renames Jacob at Peniel: “thou hast power with God and with men, and hast prevailed” (32:28). Rachel’s wrestling anticipates her husband’s, yet the two stories differ. Rachel names her own victory over a human rival; at Peniel the divine Wrestler, whom Hosea identifies with the Angel and the LORD God of hosts (Hosea 12:3–5), names Jacob after Jacob has been brought to clinging dependence. One kind of prevailing comes from outdoing others; the other comes from being humbled before God.

Rachel’s claim of victory is also premature. Leah had four sons of her own, and more were coming. Two sons by proxy did not end the contest; the next verses show Leah responding with the same method. Envy never reaches the finish line it imagines. Rivalry that is fed by success only demands another round.

Rachel’s words also show how easily religious language can be enlisted in a rivalry. By framing her contest with Leah as “wrestlings of God,” she gives her own cause divine colouring. People of faith are not immune to this temptation. Family quarrels, church disputes, and personal ambitions can all be described as battles for God when they are really battles for status. The question is not whether God’s name is used but whether His will is sought.

Naphtali’s later blessing is gentle: he is a hind let loose that gives goodly words (49:21). God was able to bring grace out of a name born in rivalry, and Christ would spend much of His Galilean ministry in the territory of Naphtali, bringing light to those who sat in darkness (Matthew 4:13–16).

wordNotes.term: נַפְתּוּלֵי אֱלֹהִים נִפְתַּלְתִּי (naftule ʾElohim niftalti) — with great wrestlings have I wrestled
wordNotes.explanation: The verb patal means to twist or wrestle. Adding ʾElohim can intensify the noun (“mighty wrestlings”) or describe a struggle concerning God. The cognate wordplay gives the name Naphtali, “my wrestling.”

wordNotes.term: יָכֹלְתִּי (yakholti) — I have prevailed
wordNotes.explanation: Yakol means to be able or to overcome. The same verb explains Jacob’s new name Israel, linking Rachel’s rivalry with the far deeper struggle at the Jabbok, where Jacob prevailed only by being broken and blessed.

verses.bibleText: When Leah saw that she had left bearing, she took Zilpah her maid, and gave her Jacob to wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“When Leah saw that she had left bearing” looks back to 29:35, where after Judah’s birth she “left bearing.” The births through Bilhah and those that follow through Zilpah likely overlap in time with Leah’s own; the narrator groups them by mother rather than in strict sequence. Leah had borne four sons, yet the pause in her childbearing, together with Rachel’s new success, unsettled her.

She answers in kind: “she took Zilpah her maid, and gave her Jacob to wife.” Envy had passed from one sister to the other. Rachel’s scheme provoked Leah to imitate it, and the household now held four women bearing children to one man. Leah had less reason than Rachel to use such means, for she was already the mother of four sons. Jacob again complies without recorded protest. Having accepted one handmaid, he seems not to question a second, and the path of compromise grows easier with each step.

This is how rivalry spreads. One person’s method becomes another’s justification, and both are drawn further from trust. Leah had once reached a high point of faith when she named Judah, saying, “Now will I praise the LORD” (29:35). Here, faced with a silence in her own fruitfulness, she turns from praise to competition. Believers can lose the peace of yesterday’s worship when they begin comparing their portion with another’s. Her earlier confession had rested on God’s faithfulness; her present move rests on her maid’s fertility. The shift is subtle but real, and it shows how quickly a heart that has rested in God can return to self-reliance when circumstances change.

wordNotes.term: עָמְדָה מִלֶּדֶת (ʿamedah milledet) — she had left bearing
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “she stood still from bearing.” The verb ʿamad, “to stand,” pictures a halt rather than permanent barrenness. The same expression in 29:35 links this verse back to the end of Leah’s first group of sons.

verses.bibleText: And Zilpah Leah's maid bare Jacob a son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Zilpah Leah’s maid bare Jacob a son.” The verse mirrors verse 5 almost word for word, and the parallel is intentional. The narrator is setting the two sisters’ strategies side by side so that their moves read like turns in a game.

Zilpah, like Bilhah, is silent. She was Laban’s gift to Leah at the wedding (29:24), and now she becomes the mother of a tribe in Israel. God’s purpose to multiply Jacob’s seed moves forward even through arrangements He did not design.

wordNotes.term: זִלְפָּה (Zilpah) — Zilpah
wordNotes.explanation: The meaning of the name is uncertain, and it is wiser not to build on guesses. What matters in the narrative is her role: Leah’s personal maid, given by Laban, through whom Gad and Asher were born and counted to Leah.

verses.bibleText: And Leah said, A troop cometh: and she called his name Gad.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Leah greets the birth with an exclamation: “A troop cometh: and she called his name Gad.” The KJV follows a traditional reading of the Hebrew. The written text has a single word, bagad, which most naturally means “with good fortune” or “how fortunate,” while the marginal reading of the scribes divides it as “fortune has come.” The Greek Old Testament rendered it “in good fortune.” Either way the name Gad is linked with luck or fortune.

The notable absence is God. At the births of Reuben, Simeon, and Judah, Leah spoke of the LORD seeing, hearing, and receiving praise (29:32–35). Here she speaks only of good fortune. Elsewhere in Scripture Gad appears as the name of a pagan deity of fortune whom apostate Israel worshipped (Isaiah 65:11), though Leah need not have had a god in mind. Her words simply reflect a shift from thanksgiving to satisfaction in a successful plan. The child was God’s gift; the mother described him as luck. A believer may receive real gifts from God and still describe them in the vocabulary of chance, missing the hand that gave them.

Leah’s exclamation is understandable in human terms. After a season without children she suddenly had another son in her household, and relief spilled into words. Yet the narrator sets her words beside her earlier confessions so that the reader can hear the difference. Thanksgiving names the Giver; mere happiness names the gift.

The KJV’s “troop” is not without echo. In Jacob’s final blessing he plays on the name: “Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last” (49:19). The tribe settled east of the Jordan and became known for its warriors (1 Chronicles 12:8). God gave the son a future far larger than his mother’s exclamation.

wordNotes.term: בָּגָד / בָּא גָד (bagad / ba gad) — a troop cometh
wordNotes.explanation: The consonantal text reads bagad, “with fortune,” while the scribal reading divides it as ba gad, “fortune has come.” Gad means fortune; the KJV’s “troop” reflects a later tradition associating the name with gedud, “band,” the very wordplay used in Jacob’s blessing.

verses.bibleText: And Zilpah Leah's maid bare Jacob a second son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Zilpah Leah’s maid bare Jacob a second son.” Once again the narrator uses the formula from Bilhah’s second son (v. 7), keeping the contest evenly balanced on the page: two sons for Rachel through Bilhah, two for Leah through Zilpah.

The repetition also shows how quickly the family was growing. The household that Jacob entered alone with a staff in his hand (32:10) was becoming a company of peoples, as Isaac had prayed (28:3).

wordNotes.term: בֵּן שֵׁנִי (ben sheni) — a second son
wordNotes.explanation: The ordinal sheni, “second,” recurs from verse 7. Such counting makes the list read like a tally in the sisters’ competition while also tracing the steady fulfilment of God’s promise of many descendants.

verses.bibleText: And Leah said, Happy am I, for the daughters will call me blessed: and she called his name Asher.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Happy am I, for the daughters will call me blessed: and she called his name Asher.” Leah’s words celebrate success in the eyes of other women. The “daughters” are the women of the community, who will count her fortunate as a mother of many sons. In that world such esteem was precious, and Leah, unloved by her husband, longed for any recognition she could find.

Again she does not mention God. Her joy rests on what others will say. The happiness she claims is real as far as it goes, yet it stands on a fragile base. Public admiration could not give her Jacob’s heart, and later in the chapter she is still bargaining for his presence (v. 16). The praise of the women of the village was a poor substitute for the praise she had once offered God at Judah’s birth.

The vocabulary of Leah’s cry anticipates a far richer song. Mary, carrying the promised Son, said, “from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed” (Luke 1:48). Mary’s blessedness flowed from what “he that is mighty” had done; Leah’s from the success of her rivalry. The same human hope to be called blessed finds its true fulfilment only when God is its source.

The word Leah uses belongs to the family of ʾashre, “blessed is the man,” which opens the Psalter (Psalm 1:1). Scripture teaches that the truly happy are those who walk with God and trust Him, whatever others think. Moses’ later blessing on Asher speaks of oil, strength, and security (Deuteronomy 33:24–25), God’s gifts surpassing a mother’s hopes. Leah would discover that the approval of the daughters of Haran mattered far less than the approval of the God who had seen her from the beginning.

wordNotes.term: בְּאָשְׁרִי … אִשְּׁרוּנִי (beʾoshri … ʾishsheruni) — happy am I … will call me blessed
wordNotes.explanation: Both words come from the root ʾashar, related to ʾashre, “blessed” or “happy.” The verb in the piel means to pronounce someone fortunate. The Greek Old Testament uses makarizō, the very verb found in Mary’s song, which shows how the idea is taken up and deepened in the New Testament.

verses.bibleText: And Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah. Then Rachel said to Leah, Give me, I pray thee, of thy son's mandrakes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The scene shifts to the fields: “Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field, and brought them unto his mother Leah.” In upper Mesopotamia the wheat harvest fell in late spring. Reuben, now a boy old enough to roam the fields, found a plant with fragrant yellow fruit and a thick forked root. The mandrake was prized across the ancient Near East as a love charm and a remedy for barrenness, and its very name in Hebrew sounds like the word for love.

Reuben brings them to his mother. As Leah’s firstborn he had every reason to want her honoured in the household. It is a small act of a son’s loyalty, but it also shows how the children were being drawn into the mothers’ rivalry. Later Reuben would seek his own place in the family by wrongful means (35:22), and the tension between Leah’s sons and Rachel’s would grow until it nearly cost Joseph his life. The innocent gift of a child to his mother became a prize in the contest of the tent.

Rachel hears of the find and asks at once, “Give me, I pray thee, of thy son’s mandrakes.” The request is polite but urgent. Rachel, who had demanded children from Jacob, now seeks them from a plant. Her desire reveals how much the pagan atmosphere of her father’s house still shaped her; she would later steal Laban’s household gods (31:19). The reader is set up to watch whether the mandrakes or God will be the giver of life.

The detail that Reuben found the mandrakes “in the field” during harvest connects the household’s quarrel with ordinary work. Life went on: wheat was reaped, flocks were tended, children played in the fields. Into that everyday setting the rivalry intruded, turning a child’s discovery into a bargaining chip. Unresolved envy rarely stays in one corner of life; it colours meals, work, and even the gifts of children.

The narrator’s answer comes swiftly. Leah, who parts with the mandrakes, conceives; Rachel, who receives them, remains barren for some time longer. When Rachel finally bears, it is because “God remembered” her (v. 22). Every attempt to find fruitfulness in charms, techniques, or human cleverness meets the same rebuke: life belongs to God.

wordNotes.term: דּוּדָאִים (dudaʾim) — mandrakes
wordNotes.explanation: The word is related in sound to dodim, “love,” and so suggests “love-apples.” The plant, Mandragora officinarum, has a strong scent and was used as an aphrodisiac and fertility aid. The Song of Solomon mentions its fragrance among the delights of love.

wordNotes.term: בִּימֵי קְצִיר־חִטִּים (bime qetsir-chittim) — in the days of wheat harvest
wordNotes.explanation: Agricultural seasons served as a calendar. Wheat harvest came after barley, in late spring, and later marked the Feast of Weeks. The note places the scene in the busy season when the whole household worked in the fields.

verses.bibleText: And she said unto her, Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son's mandrakes also? And Rachel said, Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son's mandrakes.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Leah’s reply bursts with years of pain: “Is it a small matter that thou hast taken my husband? and wouldest thou take away my son’s mandrakes also?” She speaks as though Rachel were the intruder. In fact Leah had been the one substituted on the wedding night, and Rachel the bride Jacob loved. Yet from Leah’s side, she was the first wife whose husband’s heart belonged to another. Each sister felt robbed by the other. Long-nursed grievance makes every fresh request feel like another theft. Leah could not hear Rachel’s plea without hearing years of rejection behind it.

Rachel’s answer is a bargain: “Therefore he shall lie with thee to night for thy son’s mandrakes.” It appears that Rachel, as the favoured wife, controlled Jacob’s nights. She trades a night with her husband for a fertility charm. The marriage bed, which God gave as a covenant bond of love (2:24), has become a commodity exchanged between rivals. The verb chosen for “lie with” appears elsewhere in Genesis mostly in scenes of wrong or force, and its use here hints at how far the relationship has fallen.

There is also an echo of Jacob’s past. Jacob once bought a birthright with a bowl of stew (25:29–34); now he is himself bought for a handful of fruit. The deceiver who traded on another’s hunger is traded by his wives. God’s discipline often lets people experience from the other side what they once did to others.

The verse lays bare the poverty of a home where love has been replaced by competition. Neither sister obtains what she most wants by this deal. Leah gains a night, not her husband’s affection; Rachel gains mandrakes, not a child. Only God’s gracious intervention in the next verses breaks the deadlock. The sisters had become, in effect, traders in their husband’s affections, and the children watched and learned.

wordNotes.term: הַמְעַט קַחְתֵּךְ (hameʿat qachtekh) — is it a small matter that thou hast taken
wordNotes.explanation: The question hameʿat, “is it too little?” introduces an indignant protest that one wrong is being added to another. Moses uses the same form against Korah’s company, and the phrase always signals exasperation at a demand for more.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob came out of the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him, and said, Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son's mandrakes. And he lay with her that night.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Jacob came out of the field in the evening, and Leah went out to meet him.” The patriarch returns tired from a day with the flocks and is met by a wife announcing a contract: “Thou must come in unto me; for surely I have hired thee with my son’s mandrakes.” He is not consulted. “And he lay with her that night.” The man who once plotted to seize birthright and blessing now appears passive, moved by the arrangements of others. There is no mention of Jacob’s feelings or wishes; the narrative presents him as an object passed between his wives.

The key word is “hired.” The same root runs through Jacob’s story with Laban: “what shall thy wages be?” (29:15), and it will return when Jacob’s flock wages are fixed (30:28–33). Laban turned family relationships into wage agreements, and now the spirit of his house has entered Jacob’s marriage. Leah speaks of her husband as a hired labourer. The word sums up what had gone wrong in the family: affection and covenant faithfulness replaced by bargaining.

Yet Leah’s eagerness also reveals her longing. She goes out to meet him before he can reach Rachel’s tent. She is not seeking a charm but the presence of the husband she had hoped would love her (29:32). Her request, sad in its form, is the cry of a neglected wife. Her boldness in going out to meet him shows how much she wanted to be chosen, even if only by contract.

God sees what lies beneath the transaction. In the next verse He hearkens to Leah, as He had seen her affliction from the beginning (29:31). The narrative does not excuse the bargaining, but it shows that God’s mercy reaches into even such tangled moments. Grace is not hired; it is given to the needy.

wordNotes.term: שָׂכֹר שְׂכַרְתִּיךָ (sakhor sekhartikha) — surely I have hired thee
wordNotes.explanation: The infinitive before the verb intensifies it: “I have truly hired you.” Sakhar means to hire for wages, and the noun sakhar, “wages, reward,” becomes the name Issachar. The root binds together Jacob’s labour for Laban, the mandrake deal, and the flock contract.

verses.bibleText: And God hearkened unto Leah, and she conceived, and bare Jacob the fifth son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God hearkened unto Leah, and she conceived, and bare Jacob the fifth son.” The sentence overturns the expectations of the previous verses. The mandrakes went to Rachel, yet it is Leah who conceives. The narrator does not say that the night or the plant produced the child; he says God hearkened.

The phrase also corrects any notion that Leah’s pregnancy was merely the natural result of a night purchased by mandrakes. Many nights had passed in the household without conception. What made this one fruitful was God’s attention to a woman whose deepest cry was for love and acceptance.

To hearken implies that Leah had been praying, though her prayer is not recorded. Behind her bargaining lay a heart still turned toward the God who had seen her affliction (29:31–33). The verb echoes the name of her second son, Simeon, given because “the LORD hath heard.” God had not stopped listening to the unloved wife.

The verse is a lesson in where to look for life. The same mercy that saw Hagar, heard Ishmael’s cry, and would answer Hannah stands behind Leah’s fifth son. Human devices may surround a blessing, but they do not produce it. God’s hearing comes first, and conception follows. The New Testament speaks in the same way of God, who gives to all life and breath (Acts 17:25), and who hears those who call on Him in their need. Leah’s fifth son came after she had given up the mandrakes, a detail the narrator does not need to underline.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׁמַע אֱלֹהִים אֶל־לֵאָה (vayyishmaʿ ʾElohim ʾel-Leʾah) — God hearkened unto Leah
wordNotes.explanation: Shamaʿ ʾel means to listen favourably and respond. It implies a prayer or cry that reached God. The same verb lies in Simeon’s name and in Ishmael’s, both born from God’s attention to the afflicted.

verses.bibleText: And Leah said, God hath given me my hire, because I have given my maiden to my husband: and she called his name Issachar.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Leah names the child Issachar and explains, “God hath given me my hire, because I have given my maiden to my husband.” The word “hire” takes up the bargain of verse 16. Leah sees the birth as a wage paid by God, and she links it not to the mandrakes but to her earlier act of giving Zilpah to Jacob.

Her theology is mixed. She rightly attributes the child to God, and she does not credit the mandrakes. But she treats her handmaid scheme, born of rivalry, as a deed of merit that God has now rewarded. It was Leah who drew this conclusion; the narrator only reported that God hearkened. Scripture often records the interpretations of its characters without endorsing them, and readers must distinguish between what God did and what people thought He was doing. God can give good gifts even when His people misunderstand why He gave them.

The Psalms speak of children as God’s reward using the same word: “the fruit of the womb is his reward” (Psalm 127:3). There the reward is pure gift, flowing from God’s kindness and not from the parents’ deserving. Leah’s son was such a gift. God’s generosity is not a wage owed for clever choices but grace given to those who did not earn it. Paul makes the same distinction when he contrasts wages reckoned as a debt with grace counted freely to the one who believes (Romans 4:4–5).

The tribe of Issachar would later be described as a strong donkey bending to labour (49:14–15), and in David’s day as men who understood the times and knew what Israel ought to do (1 Chronicles 12:32). A name formed from a contract became, in God’s hands, a tribe marked by faithful service and wisdom.

wordNotes.term: שְׂכָרִי … יִשָּׂשכָר (sekhari … Yissakhar) — my hire … Issachar
wordNotes.explanation: Sakhar means wages or reward. Leah’s phrase and the name share the root; Issachar is commonly understood as “there is reward” or “man of hire.” The Hebrew spelling with a doubled s-sound has puzzled scribes, but the link to sakhar is clear and deliberate.

verses.bibleText: And Leah conceived again, and bare Jacob the sixth son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Leah conceived again, and bare Jacob the sixth son.” With this birth Leah becomes the mother of half of the twelve tribes. The unloved wife, the one Jacob did not choose, has borne Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and now a sixth.

The simple record carries real weight. From Leah’s sons would come the priestly tribe of Levi and the royal tribe of Judah, through whom the Messiah would be born (Matthew 1:2–3). God’s choice once again rests on the overlooked.

wordNotes.term: בֵּן־שִׁשִּׁי (ben-shishshi) — the sixth son
wordNotes.explanation: The ordinal marks Leah’s total of six sons, a number she herself mentions in the next verse as grounds for her hope. It completes her share, half of the twelve sons of Israel.

verses.bibleText: And Leah said, God hath endued me with a good dowry; now will my husband dwell with me, because I have born him six sons: and she called his name Zebulun.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Leah’s speech at Zebulun’s birth joins thanksgiving and longing: “God hath endued me with a good dowry; now will my husband dwell with me, because I have born him six sons.” The first half is gratitude. A dowry was the gift that came with a bride into a marriage; Leah sees her sons as God’s rich endowment, a wealth she brings to her husband.

The second half reveals the ache that had never left her. After Levi she had said, “Now this time will my husband be joined unto me” (29:34). Now, three sons later, she says much the same: “now will my husband dwell with me.” The verb suggests honour and settled residence, the hope that Jacob would treat her as his true and esteemed wife. Six sons had not yet won his heart. Her hope is touching and sad at once. Six times she had hoped, and the hope had not yet been answered as she wished.

Leah’s story is a mirror for anyone who tries to earn love by performance. She multiplied what she thought would make her valued, and still the love she longed for seemed out of reach. God, however, had already valued her. He had seen her affliction, hearkened to her, and made her the mother of the priestly and royal lines. When she was finally laid to rest, it was in the family tomb at Machpelah beside Jacob (49:31), while Rachel was buried by the roadside. In the end Leah had the place she desired, though not in the way she had planned. Her place in Israel’s memory would rest not on winning Jacob but on God’s faithfulness to her.

Zebulun’s tribe would later dwell by the sea and be named, with Naphtali, as the land where a great light dawned in Christ’s ministry (Isaiah 9:1–2). God’s endowment far exceeded what Leah could see.

wordNotes.term: זְבָדַנִי … זֵבֶד טוֹב (zevadani … zeved tov) — hath endued me with a good dowry
wordNotes.explanation: The verb zavad, “to endow,” with its cognate noun zeved, “gift,” appears only here in the Old Testament, though it survives in names such as Zabdi and Zebadiah. It pictures God as the generous giver of a bridal gift.

wordNotes.term: יִזְבְּלֵנִי (yizbeleni) — will dwell with me
wordNotes.explanation: Zaval is related to zevul, “lofty abode,” as in Solomon’s “house to dwell in.” Leah hopes Jacob will honour her with his settled presence. The name Zebulun combines this verb with the sound of zavad.

verses.bibleText: And afterwards she bare a daughter, and called her name Dinah.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And afterwards she bare a daughter, and called her name Dinah.” The word “afterwards” suggests an interval following Zebulun’s birth. Unlike the sons, Dinah receives no explanation of her name. The record of daughters in Genesis is selective, and Jacob had other daughters (37:35; 46:7), yet Dinah alone is named, for her story will be told in chapter 34. Her birth after Leah’s six sons rounds off Leah’s family at seven children, a number that suggests fullness.

Her name comes from the same root as Dan, meaning judgment or vindication. Leah’s last child thus echoes Rachel’s first. The narrator offers no commentary, but readers of chapter 34 will remember the name when Dinah is wronged and her brothers take vengeance into their own hands. Vindication sought by human violence would bring Jacob great sorrow.

The brief mention of Dinah is a gentle reminder that God’s record includes those the culture overlooked. A daughter in a household that counted sons is still named in the sacred text. In Christ, sons and daughters alike are heirs of the promise (Galatians 3:28–29). Her brief appearance also completes the picture of a growing household: eleven sons and a daughter by the time Joseph is born.

wordNotes.term: דִּינָה (Dinah) — Dinah
wordNotes.explanation: From din, “to judge,” the name may mean “judgment” or “vindicated.” It shares its root with Dan, Rachel’s first son by Bilhah. No explanation is given, unlike her brothers, so it is best not to press a meaning beyond the evident echo of Dan.

verses.bibleText: And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And God remembered Rachel, and God hearkened to her, and opened her womb.” This is the turning point of the whole birth narrative. Three verbs, each with God as subject, stand against all the human striving that came before. Rachel had demanded children from Jacob, used her handmaid, and bargained for mandrakes. Now God acts.

For God to remember does not mean He had forgotten. In Scripture it signals that God turns to act on behalf of someone in fulfilment of His covenant purposes. The same words opened the end of the flood: “God remembered Noah” (8:1). God remembered Abraham and delivered Lot (19:29). He would remember His covenant and deliver Israel from Egypt (Exodus 2:24), and He remembered Hannah, who bore Samuel (1 Samuel 1:19). Rachel stands in a line of people at the end of their resources whom God visited with deliverance.

“God hearkened to her” implies that Rachel had at last turned to prayer. Her earlier words had been complaints to Jacob and claims of victory over Leah. The narrative implies a change: the wife who had sought help from her husband, her maid, and a plant now brought her need to God. Whether this came quickly or after long waiting, the timing was His. Faith received what impatience could not seize. Waiting had done its work: Rachel had come to the end of her own resources and found that God had been near all along.

“Opened her womb” matches the language used of Leah at the start (29:31), forming a frame around the whole account. The LORD who opened Leah’s womb when she was unloved now opens Rachel’s when she is barren. Between those two statements stand every scheme of the household, and none of them is credited with a single conception that the narrator attributes to God. The mandrakes vanish from the story.

This verse speaks to all who wait. God does not always answer as quickly as people wish, nor always with what they request. But He remembers. The God who remembered Rachel remembered His promise of a Saviour and, “when the fulness of the time was come,” sent forth His Son (Galatians 4:4). Every delay in the history of redemption has ended in the same way: God remembers, and the promise moves forward.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים (vayyizkor ʾElohim) — and God remembered
wordNotes.explanation: Zakhar is more than recollection; it means to call to mind with the intent to act. When God is the subject it introduces deliverance or covenant faithfulness, as at the flood and the exodus. The thief on the cross asked Jesus to remember him in this saving sense.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְתַּח אֶת־רַחְמָהּ (vayyiftach ʾet-rachmah) — and opened her womb
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase uses patach, “to open,” with rechem, “womb.” It appears for Leah in 29:31 and here for Rachel, framing the birth narrative. The noun rechem is related to rachamim, “compassion,” a fitting association when God acts in mercy.

verses.bibleText: And she conceived, and bare a son; and said, God hath taken away my reproach:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she conceived, and bare a son; and said, God hath taken away my reproach.” For Rachel, the deepest pain of barrenness had been shame. In that culture a childless wife was not merely pitied; she was often despised, and her condition was read as a sign of disfavour. Rachel had lived for years beside a sister who bore son after son, and every birth deepened her humiliation.

Now she gives God the credit. The reproach is removed not by her schemes but by God’s gift. Her confession contrasts with her earlier words at the births of Bilhah’s sons, where she spoke of vindication and victory over her sister. Here she speaks simply of shame lifted. Something had changed in Rachel’s heart through the long waiting. The woman who once said, “I have prevailed,” now says, “God hath taken away.”

Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist, used almost the same words when she conceived in old age: “Thus hath the Lord dealt with me … to take away my reproach among men” (Luke 1:25). Both women experienced God as the One who removes shame. The New Testament carries that work further. Christ “endured the cross, despising the shame” (Hebrews 12:2) so that those who trust Him would not be put to shame (Romans 10:11). The deepest reproach of humanity, the disgrace of sin, is taken away by the Son God gave.

The verse also counsels gentleness. Many who long for children never receive them, and no one should read their childlessness as God’s reproach. Rachel’s story shows that God sees the shame others place upon the barren and that His verdict, not the community’s, is the one that counts. Those who bear such sorrow may find in Rachel’s story the assurance that God knows their reproach by name.

wordNotes.term: אָסַף אֱלֹהִים אֶת־חֶרְפָּתִי (ʾasaf ʾElohim ʾet-cherpati) — God hath taken away my reproach
wordNotes.explanation: Cherpah means disgrace, scorn, or taunting. ʾAsaf usually means to gather; here it means to gather up and remove. The verb sounds like the name Joseph and supplies the first of two wordplays on his name. Isaiah promises that God will cause Israel to forget the reproach of her widowhood.

verses.bibleText: And she called his name Joseph; and said, The LORD shall add to me another son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she called his name Joseph; and said, The LORD shall add to me another son.” Rachel gives a second explanation for the name, this time looking forward. Joseph, sounding like the verb “add,” becomes a prayer for another child. The one gift prompts hope for more.

For the first time in the chapter Rachel uses the covenant name, the LORD. Earlier she spoke only of God (ʾElohim), the Creator and Judge. Now, having received the child she longed for, she speaks of the God who had bound Himself in covenant to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The shift fits the change in her heart. Her prayer would be answered, but at great cost: Benjamin’s birth on the road to Bethlehem would end her life (35:16–19).

Joseph’s name would prove prophetic in ways Rachel could not foresee. The son who added to her joy would be taken away by his brothers’ jealousy and then added back to his father’s arms after years of grief (45:26–28). Through Joseph God would save the entire family from famine, preserving the line of promise. In this he became a living picture of the greater Son, rejected by His brothers yet exalted to save them (Acts 7:9–14). Joseph would be lost, mourned, and restored, and in his restoration the family would find life.

Rachel’s naming speech is the last of the chapter’s birth speeches, and it is the first that ends in a petition rather than a boast or a claim. That shift is significant. The mother who had once demanded children from her husband now asks them from the LORD. Her desire for more is not condemned; it is directed to the right Giver. Joseph’s very name became a standing prayer in the household, a daily reminder that the future of the family lay in God’s hands.

The birth also marks a turning point in Jacob’s story. As soon as Joseph is born, Jacob asks to go home (v. 25). Yet Rachel’s firstborn would not inherit the messianic line; that honour went to Judah, son of Leah. God’s purposes rarely follow human favouritism. He gave Rachel her son and kept the promise of the Seed moving through the unloved wife, showing that grace, not preference, governs His plan.

wordNotes.term: יוֹסֵף … יֹסֵף יְהוָה (Yosef … yosef YHWH) — Joseph … the LORD shall add
wordNotes.explanation: The name means “may he add,” from yasaf. Combined with ʾasaf in verse 23, it forms a double wordplay: God has taken away, and the LORD will add. The second explanation uses the covenant name, expressing a prayer for another son that was fulfilled in Benjamin.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when Rachel had born Joseph, that Jacob said unto Laban, Send me away, that I may go unto mine own place, and to my country.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass, when Rachel had born Joseph, that Jacob said unto Laban, Send me away, that I may go unto mine own place, and to my country.” The birth of Joseph marks a turning point. Jacob’s fourteen years of service for his wives were complete, and now that Rachel had a son, his thoughts turned homeward. Joseph’s arrival seems to have given Jacob the sense that his household was established and that it was time to return to the land God had promised.

Jacob’s words reveal his loyalty to that promise. Though he had lived in Paddan-aram for many years, married there, and raised children there, he still called Canaan “mine own place.” He had vowed at Bethel that if God brought him back in peace, the LORD would be his God (28:21). The pilgrim had not forgotten where his inheritance lay. The New Testament praises the patriarchs for this very attitude: they confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims, seeking a better, heavenly country (Hebrews 11:13–16). The longing for home that Jacob expresses is the same longing God plants in every believer who knows that this world is not the final dwelling place.

The verb “send me away” has a formal ring. Jacob asks permission to leave, as a servant would from his master. He could have slipped away, but that would have looked like theft and invited pursuit. Instead he seeks a proper release. Centuries later the same verb would ring out in Egypt: “Let my people go” (Exodus 5:1). In both cases a powerful master was unwilling to release those whose labour enriched him, and in both cases God would bring His people out with substance. In both stories the oppressor’s reluctance becomes the stage on which God shows His power to free His servants.

Jacob’s request also tests Laban’s character. A fair employer would have sent such a faithful worker away with generous provision (Deuteronomy 15:13–14). Laban’s response in the following verses shows that he had other plans.

wordNotes.term: שַׁלְּחֵנִי (shallecheni) — send me away
wordNotes.explanation: The intensive form of shalach means to release or dismiss, often with formal permission. It is the key verb of the exodus demand, “Let my people go,” and Deuteronomy uses it for releasing a servant with provision.

verses.bibleText: Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served thee, and let me go: for thou knowest my service which I have done thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Give me my wives and my children, for whom I have served thee, and let me go: for thou knowest my service which I have done thee.” Jacob’s language is weighted with the word “serve,” used three times in this verse in Hebrew. He describes his years with Laban as servitude, which in effect they had been. Fourteen years of labour had paid for his wives; he had nothing else to show for it.

That Jacob must ask for his own wives and children reveals Laban’s attitude. Legally they belonged to Jacob, but Laban seems to have regarded them as still under his authority, as he later claims: “These daughters are my daughters, and these children are my children” (31:43). Jacob appeals to what Laban himself knew: his faithful, demanding service. He would later recount it in detail, the heat by day and frost by night (31:38–40). The request is not only for permission to leave but for the recognition that his family is truly his, a recognition Laban would grudgingly concede only after God intervened (31:24, 43–44).

The verse shows Jacob as a man who had kept his side of a hard bargain. Faithfulness under an unfair master is a theme Scripture honours (Colossians 3:22–24), and God would not leave such labour unrewarded. Jacob had learned in hard service what the deceiver of earlier years had not known: that faithfulness is slow, costly, and noticed by God.

wordNotes.term: עֲבֹדָתִי אֲשֶׁר עֲבַדְתִּיךָ (ʿavodati ʾasher ʿavadtikha) — my service which I have done thee
wordNotes.explanation: ʿAvad means to work or serve, often as a servant or slave. The repeated root stresses that Jacob’s years were service, the same vocabulary later used for Israel’s bondage in Egypt and for the worship Israel would render to God when set free.

verses.bibleText: And Laban said unto him, I pray thee, if I have found favour in thine eyes, tarry: for I have learned by experience that the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban answers with courtesy: “I pray thee, if I have found favour in thine eyes, tarry.” The polite formula hides self-interest. He then makes a striking admission: “I have learned by experience that the LORD hath blessed me for thy sake.” Laban had grown rich through Jacob’s presence and knew it.

The phrase “learned by experience” translates a verb that elsewhere means to practise divination. Joseph’s silver cup is described as the one “whereby he divineth” (44:5), and the Law forbids Israel to use such practices (Leviticus 19:26). Laban, who kept household gods (31:19), may have consulted omens and concluded that Jacob’s presence was the cause of his prosperity. Some take the verb in a related sense, “I have grown rich,” which also fits the context. Either way, Laban reached the truth by a path God had forbidden, and his knowledge did not change his heart. The LORD can use even a pagan’s observations to bear witness to His faithfulness, but such observations are no model for His people.

The confession itself is remarkable. A man outside the covenant acknowledges that the LORD, the God of Abraham, has blessed him because of Jacob. God had promised Abraham that in his seed all families of the earth would be blessed (12:3; 28:14). Laban was experiencing a foretaste of that promise. The same pattern would recur when Potiphar’s house was blessed for Joseph’s sake (39:5).

Yet acknowledgment is not conversion. Laban recognised the blessing but continued to cheat the man through whom it came (31:7). Many today admit that faith has done good in the world while refusing to submit to the God behind it. True response to God’s blessing is repentance and trust, not merely an observation that it pays to keep His servants close. Jesus warned against the same divided heart: it is possible to profit from the presence of God’s people while never yielding to God Himself (Matthew 7:22–23).

wordNotes.term: נִחַשְׁתִּי (nichashti) — I have learned by experience
wordNotes.explanation: Nachash usually means to practise divination or observe omens. Joseph’s cup and the Law’s prohibition use the same verb. Some connect it with a related word meaning “to prosper.” Either reading shows Laban gaining knowledge outside the true worship of God.

wordNotes.term: בִּגְלָלֶךָ (biglalekha) — for thy sake
wordNotes.explanation: Biglal means “on account of.” It points to Jacob as the channel through whom God’s blessing flowed to Laban. The same expression describes the LORD blessing the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Appoint me thy wages, and I will give it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he said, Appoint me thy wages, and I will give it.” The offer sounds generous, but Jacob had heard similar words before. Fourteen years earlier Laban had asked, “what shall thy wages be?” (29:15) and then substituted Leah for Rachel. Laban’s invitation is less an act of generosity than a strategy to keep a profitable worker.

Jacob would later testify that Laban changed his wages ten times during the following six years (31:7, 41). An open-ended offer from a dishonest man is a trap. Jacob’s careful proposal in the following verses shows that he had learned from experience.

wordNotes.term: נָקְבָה שְׂכָרְךָ (noqvah sekharekha) — appoint me thy wages
wordNotes.explanation: Naqav means to designate or specify, literally to pierce or mark out. Laban invites Jacob to name a precise wage. The noun sakhar continues the chapter’s key word, linking this offer to Leah’s “hire.”

verses.bibleText: And he said unto him, Thou knowest how I have served thee, and how thy cattle was with me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob begins his reply by appealing to Laban’s own knowledge: “Thou knowest how I have served thee, and how thy cattle was with me.” Jacob does not need omens to prove his worth; Laban has seen it with his own eyes. The flocks had flourished under Jacob’s care, and the evidence was all around them.

The verse shows a man who lets his work speak. Jacob does not boast at length but points to what Laban could not deny. His later speech fills in what this care had cost him: sleepless nights, losses he bore himself, and attacks from wild beasts (31:38–40). Faithful labour is a form of witness. Scripture urges servants to work heartily, as to the Lord, knowing that the Lord sees and rewards (Ephesians 6:5–8).

wordNotes.term: מִקְנְךָ (miqnekha) — thy cattle
wordNotes.explanation: Miqneh means acquired property, especially livestock, from qanah, “to acquire.” In a pastoral economy it represented a man’s wealth. Jacob reminds Laban that his wealth had grown under Jacob’s care.

verses.bibleText: For it was little which thou hadst before I came, and it is now increased unto a multitude; and the LORD hath blessed thee since my coming: and now when shall I provide for mine own house also?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob makes his case: “For it was little which thou hadst before I came, and it is now increased unto a multitude; and the LORD hath blessed thee since my coming.” The contrast between “little” and “multitude” is sharp. Laban’s modest holdings had multiplied under Jacob’s hand. The verb for “increased” pictures something bursting through its limits. It is the same word God used at Bethel when He promised that Jacob’s seed would “spread abroad” to the west, east, north, and south (28:14).

Jacob attributes the increase to God: “the LORD hath blessed thee since my coming.” The phrase “since my coming” is literally “at my foot,” meaning wherever Jacob went. He was not claiming credit for himself alone. He recognised that God’s presence, promised at Bethel, had followed him into Laban’s fields. This is Jacob’s first recorded acknowledgment of God’s blessing since he arrived in Haran.

Jacob’s testimony is also an implicit rebuke. Laban had needed omens to discover what was obvious; Jacob simply states what God has done. Those who walk with God learn to read His blessing in the ordinary record of their days, without consulting forbidden powers. The difference between the two men is not that one saw the blessing and the other did not, but that one gave God the credit while the other tried to hold on to the channel of blessing for his own profit.

Then comes the question that had been building for years: “and now when shall I provide for mine own house also?” Jacob had a large family and nothing to support them. He had enriched another man’s house while his own remained empty-handed. Scripture recognises that a man must care for his own household (1 Timothy 5:8); there is nothing selfish in Jacob’s desire to provide for his wives and children. His question was a just one, and God would answer it.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְרֹץ לָרֹב (vayyifrots larov) — it is now increased unto a multitude
wordNotes.explanation: Parats means to break out or burst forth. It describes sudden, abundant growth. God used it at Bethel when He promised Jacob’s seed would spread abroad, and it returns in verse 43 when Jacob himself increases exceedingly.

wordNotes.term: לְרַגְלִי (leragli) — since my coming
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “at my foot,” the phrase means “wherever I went” or “in my steps.” It pictures blessing following Jacob’s path, as God had promised to keep him in all places whither he went.

verses.bibleText: And he said, What shall I give thee? And Jacob said, Thou shalt not give me any thing: if thou wilt do this thing for me, I will again feed and keep thy flock:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Laban repeats his question: “What shall I give thee?” And Jacob surprises him: “Thou shalt not give me any thing.” Jacob wanted no gift from Laban’s hand. Having experienced Laban’s “gifts” before, he preferred to rely on a clear arrangement whose results would depend on the flocks themselves, and so ultimately on God. The question itself was unusual for Laban, a man far more accustomed to taking than to giving.

His condition is simple: “if thou wilt do this thing for me, I will again feed and keep thy flock.” Jacob offered to continue as shepherd, guarding and pasturing Laban’s animals. The word “keep” suggests protection, the faithful watch of a shepherd over his charge. He was willing to stay longer, but on terms that would let God’s blessing be seen.

Jacob’s refusal of a gift has a certain dignity. Abraham had refused to take anything from the king of Sodom, lest it be said that a man had made him rich (14:23). Jacob likewise would not owe his prosperity to Laban. Whatever came to him would come from the God who had promised to be with him. Jacob’s confidence in God’s provision was still mixed with his own ingenuity, as the following verses show, but the direction of his trust was right.

wordNotes.term: לֹא־תִתֶּן־לִי מְאוּמָה (loʾ-titten-li meʾumah) — thou shalt not give me any thing
wordNotes.explanation: Meʾumah means “anything at all.” Jacob’s emphatic refusal echoes Abram’s refusal of Sodom’s goods. He would receive no handout but would let the increase of the flock, under God’s blessing, determine his wage.

wordNotes.term: אֶשְׁמֹר (ʾeshmor) — keep
wordNotes.explanation: Shamar means to guard or watch over. Applied to a shepherd it describes protective care; the same verb describes how God would keep Jacob in all places he went.

verses.bibleText: I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob now spells out his terms: “I will pass through all thy flock to day, removing from thence all the speckled and spotted cattle, and all the brown cattle among the sheep, and the spotted and speckled among the goats: and of such shall be my hire.” In that region sheep were normally white and goats normally black or dark brown. Animals with unusual colouring, dark sheep or goats marked with white, were the exception. Jacob was choosing what Laban would have considered the least valuable portion.

Jacob’s proposal therefore seemed modest. He asked only for the off-coloured animals, a small portion of the whole. Laban would keep the great majority. The separation would also make the division easy to see: anyone could tell at a glance which animals were Jacob’s. In the ancient world a shepherd’s share commonly came from the increase of the flock, so the principle of the bargain was familiar.

The proposal seems to mean that the existing off-coloured animals would be set aside as Jacob’s starting stock and that future offspring with such markings would also be his. Whatever the exact details, Jacob was staking his livelihood on what God would do with the flocks. If God did not bless, he would have little; if God blessed, the evidence would be plain.

Jacob’s choice also exposed him to risk. If the flocks produced few marked animals, he would remain poor while serving another six years. By accepting a wage dependent on the unusual, Jacob made his future impossible to explain apart from God. Laban would have no grounds to claim that Jacob had taken what belonged to him, and Jacob would have no grounds to boast that his own hands had made him rich.

The arrangement is an act of reliance on God, even if Jacob’s methods would later be mixed with human ingenuity. He had seen God prosper Laban for his sake. Now he placed his own future in the same hands, trusting that the God of Bethel would provide for his household.

wordNotes.term: נָקֹד וְטָלוּא (naqod vetaluʾ) — speckled and spotted
wordNotes.explanation: Naqod describes animals marked with small dots, taluʾ those with larger patches. Together they describe the irregular colouring Jacob claimed as his wage. The terms recur in chapter 31 when Jacob recounts how God transferred Laban’s flock to him.

wordNotes.term: חוּם (chum) — brown
wordNotes.explanation: Chum denotes a dark, perhaps black or deep brown, colour. It appears only in this passage, describing sheep that departed from the usual white fleece. Normal white sheep were proverbial for whiteness.

verses.bibleText: So shall my righteousness answer for me in time to come, when it shall come for my hire before thy face: every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats, and brown among the sheep, that shall be counted stolen with me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob adds a clause that makes the agreement easy to audit: “So shall my righteousness answer for me in time to come, when it shall come for my hire before thy face: every one that is not speckled and spotted among the goats, and brown among the sheep, that shall be counted stolen with me.” Any normally coloured animal found in Jacob’s flock would be proof of theft. His honesty would be visible in every animal he owned. No hidden reckoning would be needed.

The word “righteousness” here means integrity in fulfilling an obligation. Jacob was staking his reputation on the transparency of the arrangement. For a man whose name had once been bound up with deception, this was a striking commitment. He was offering to be judged by plain evidence.

Jacob would later appeal to this very integrity. When Laban pursued him and searched his goods, Jacob could say that nothing of Laban’s had been found and that he had borne every loss himself (31:36–39). Uprightness in work, even under an unfair employer, gives a clear conscience and an answer when one is accused. Paul likewise urged believers to provide things honest in the sight of all men (Romans 12:17).

wordNotes.term: וְעָנְתָה־בִּי צִדְקָתִי (veʿanetah-bi tsidqati) — so shall my righteousness answer for me
wordNotes.explanation: Tsedaqah, “righteousness,” here means faithfulness to the terms of an agreement. ʿAnah, “to answer,” is a legal term for testifying. Jacob’s honesty would bear witness on his behalf, like a reliable witness in court.

wordNotes.term: גָּנוּב (ganuv) — stolen
wordNotes.explanation: The passive participle of ganav, “to steal,” marks what would count as theft. The same verb later describes Rachel’s theft of Laban’s gods and Laban’s accusation against Jacob, giving the clause an ironic echo.

verses.bibleText: And Laban said, Behold, I would it might be according to thy word.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Laban said, Behold, I would it might be according to thy word.” Laban accepts eagerly. In Hebrew his reply begins with two particles that express enthusiasm, something like “Good! Let it be as you say.” The terms seemed to favour him heavily, and he was quick to seal them before Jacob could change his mind.

Yet Laban’s ready agreement did not mean he intended to keep it honestly. The next verses show him acting at once to rig the outcome in his favour. His quick “yes” was the response of a man who saw an advantage and planned to make it larger.

wordNotes.term: הֵן לוּ יְהִי כִדְבָרֶךָ (hen lu yehi khidvarekha) — Behold, I would it might be according to thy word
wordNotes.explanation: Hen, “behold,” and lu, “oh that,” combine to express eager consent. Laban’s enthusiasm reveals his calculation, not generosity; the deal looked as if it would cost him almost nothing.

verses.bibleText: And he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, and all the she goats that were speckled and spotted, and every one that had some white in it, and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he removed that day the he goats that were ringstraked and spotted, and all the she goats that were speckled and spotted, and every one that had some white in it, and all the brown among the sheep, and gave them into the hand of his sons.” Jacob had proposed to do the sorting himself, but Laban took charge of it. And instead of giving the off-coloured animals to Jacob as his starting flock, Laban handed them to his own sons.

The effect was to leave Jacob with only plain-coloured animals, the ones least likely to produce speckled offspring. Laban was stripping Jacob’s wage of its foundation. If any coloured animals were born now, it would be from flocks that, by appearance, had none. Laban had once again cheated Jacob, this time by narrowing the terms in his own favour. He kept the letter of his consent while emptying it of substance, the kind of dealing God’s law condemns as a false balance.

The mention of Laban’s sons is the first in the narrative. They will appear again, complaining that Jacob had taken all their father’s wealth (31:1). Laban’s greed was passing to the next generation. The father who had exchanged his daughters in marriage now enlists his sons in sharp dealing.

Yet Laban’s fraud set the stage for God’s blessing to be all the more evident. With every coloured animal removed, Jacob’s increase could not be explained by ordinary breeding from his starting stock. The word “white” here is lavan, the very sound of Laban’s name. The man who called himself “white” would see God bring the white-marked animals to Jacob.

wordNotes.term: עֲקֻדִּים (ʿaqudim) — ringstraked
wordNotes.explanation: ʿAqod describes animals with striped or banded markings, perhaps rings of colour on the legs. The word joins the list of patterns Jacob’s wage would include, and it recurs in Jacob’s dream in 31:10–12.

wordNotes.term: לָבָן (lavan) — white
wordNotes.explanation: Lavan means “white” and is identical in sound with the name Laban. The wordplay runs through the passage: the poplar (livneh) and the white streaks (levanot) all echo his name, as though Jacob is turning Laban’s own “whiteness” to his advantage.

verses.bibleText: And he set three days' journey betwixt himself and Jacob: and Jacob fed the rest of Laban's flocks.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he set three days’ journey betwixt himself and Jacob: and Jacob fed the rest of Laban’s flocks.” Laban took no chances. The distance kept the off-coloured animals far from Jacob’s flock so that no interbreeding could occur. He thought he had made the agreement worthless to Jacob.

Jacob was left with “the rest of Laban’s flocks,” the solid-coloured animals. He faithfully pastured them, as he had promised. The separation also had an unintended result: the distance would later make it possible for Jacob to depart without Laban knowing until the third day (31:22). The very precautions of the schemer became the means of his defeat. Jacob, for his part, did not abandon his post or neglect the animals left in his charge. He continued to shepherd the very flock from which his rival hoped he would gain nothing.

The verse shows how the righteous may be wronged and yet not abandoned. God would bless Jacob from the flock Laban left him, proving that prosperity comes not from favourable conditions but from the Lord who owns the cattle on a thousand hills (Psalm 50:10).

wordNotes.term: דֶּרֶךְ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים (derekh sheloshet yamim) — three days’ journey
wordNotes.explanation: A common biblical measure of distance, perhaps forty to sixty miles depending on terrain. It ensured that the flocks would not mix. The same measure later describes the gap before Laban learned of Jacob’s flight.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods.” Jacob now takes action. He peels strips of bark from fresh branches so that the white wood shows in stripes. The trees named are probably the white poplar, the almond, and the plane tree.

Jacob seems to have believed in an idea widespread in the ancient world and still common in folklore: that what a mother sees at the time of conception can mark her offspring. By placing striped rods before the animals as they mated, he hoped to produce striped and spotted young. Like Rachel with her mandrakes, he reached for a popular remedy. The belief that maternal impressions shape offspring has no basis in how life is passed from parent to young, and the narrative does not ask the reader to accept it.

The narrative itself, however, does not credit the rods with the result. In chapter 31 Jacob tells his wives what God had shown him in a dream: the rams that leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grizzled, and the Angel of God said, “I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee” (31:10–12). Jacob then declares, “God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” (31:9). The increase came from God’s blessing working through the breeding of the flock, not from the peeled sticks. Some suggest the trees contained substances that affected the animals, but the text’s own explanation is God. Jacob’s rods, then, are part of the story but not its explanation, much as the mandrakes were in the first half of the chapter.

The Hebrew is full of wordplay on Laban’s name. The poplar is livneh, the white streaks are levanot, and both sound like Laban. Colour has marked Jacob’s contests before: Esau, called Edom because of the red pottage, lost his birthright over a meal of that colour (25:30). Now a man whose very name means white faces a scheme built on white stripes. This time, though, God takes the outcome into His own hands.
