One of the trees, the almond (luz), recalls the old name of Bethel (28:19), the place where God had promised to be with him. Jacob’s tricks were feeble; the promise of Bethel was sure.

wordNotes.term: לִבְנֶה … לוּז … עַרְמוֹן (livneh … luz … ʿarmon) — poplar … hazel … chesnut
wordNotes.explanation: Livneh is usually identified as the white poplar or storax, luz as the almond, and ʿarmon as the plane tree. The KJV’s hazel and chestnut reflect older guesses. Luz is also the earlier name of Bethel, a fitting reminder of God’s promise there.

wordNotes.term: פְּצָלוֹת לְבָנוֹת (petsalot levanot) — white strakes
wordNotes.explanation: Petsalot means peeled strips, from patsal, “to peel.” Levanot, “white,” echoes Laban’s name, adding to the wordplay that runs through the scene.

verses.bibleText: And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink.” Jacob placed the peeled rods where the animals gathered, at the watering troughs. In the heat of the day the flocks came to drink, and it was often there that mating took place. Jacob arranged for the striped rods to be in view at that moment.

The verse describes Jacob’s intention: “that they should conceive.” It reports what he hoped, not what caused the result. Scripture often records the reasoning of its characters without endorsing it. Here the narrator lets the reader watch Jacob’s confidence in his technique, while chapter 31 will reveal the true source of his success. Jacob’s reasoning was the reasoning of his age, and it tells us more about Jacob than about how life is passed from one generation to the next.

The scene echoes earlier moments at wells and troughs. Jacob had first met Rachel at a well, rolling away the stone so her flock could drink (29:10). Watering places were the centre of pastoral life, where flocks were tended and agreements made. Now the trough becomes the place where Jacob schemes, yet even there God was at work beyond his understanding.

wordNotes.term: בָּרֳהָטִים בְּשִׁקֲתוֹת הַמָּיִם (barhatim beshiqatot hammayim) — in the gutters in the watering troughs
wordNotes.explanation: Rahat denotes a channel or trough for water; shoqet is a drinking trough. Together they describe the place where the animals drank, which was also where they mated. Exodus pictures the same troughs at the well where Moses met Zipporah.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּחַמְנָה (vayyechamnah) — that they should conceive
wordNotes.explanation: The verb yacham means to be in heat or to mate. It describes the animals’ breeding season and is used again in verses 39 and 41. It refers to the animals’ natural cycle, not a result of the rods.

verses.bibleText: And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted.” On the surface the plan worked: the solid-coloured animals produced multicoloured young. The narrator records the sequence without explaining it, and a careless reader might conclude that the rods caused the markings.

Chapter 31 forbids that conclusion. There Jacob tells his wives that God had shown him in a dream that the rams mating with the flock were ringstraked, speckled, and grizzled, and that the Angel of God said, “I have seen all that Laban doeth unto thee” (31:10–12). The colouring came through the breeding animals themselves, carrying traits that did not show outwardly, and through God’s overruling blessing. A mother’s sight cannot imprint markings on her offspring; the rods were powerless. The markings appeared because God had determined to repay Jacob for Laban’s injustice.

The order of events matters. Laban had removed every visibly marked animal (vv. 35–36), so the plain-coloured flock left to Jacob could produce marked young only if hidden traits were already present in them, and only in such abundance if God was directing the result. What appeared to be Jacob’s success was in fact God’s vindication of a wronged servant. The same God who opened wombs in the first half of the chapter now governs the births of the flock in the second.

Jacob himself later gave the credit to God: “Thus God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” (31:9). He had trusted his technique, but God gently taught him the real reason for his success. The rods were Jacob’s idea; the increase was God’s gift.

The passage carries a lesson for every age that seeks success through methods and secrets. Human effort has its place, and Jacob worked diligently. But when people trust their techniques, they mistake the instrument for the source. “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psalm 127:1). Jacob was learning, slowly, that the God of Bethel was the true Provider. The rods did not have to be removed for God to act; He simply did His work in spite of them.

wordNotes.term: וַתֵּלַדְןָ הַצֹּאן עֲקֻדִּים נְקֻדִּים וּטְלֻאִים (vattéladna hatstsoʾn ʿaqudim nequddim utluʾim) — brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted
wordNotes.explanation: The three adjectives repeat the colour terms of the agreement. Their reappearance in the dream of 31:10–12 shows that God, not the rods, governed which young were born marked and so became Jacob’s.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob did separate the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the ringstraked, and all the brown in the flock of Laban; and he put his own flocks by themselves, and put them not unto Laban's cattle.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob did separate the lambs, and set the faces of the flocks toward the ringstraked, and all the brown in the flock of Laban; and he put his own flocks by themselves, and put them not unto Laban’s cattle.” This verse is difficult to translate, and its details are uncertain. Jacob seems to have used the newly born multicoloured animals as a visual focus for the breeding flock, again following his belief that what the animals saw would influence their offspring.

He also kept his own growing flock separate from Laban’s. This was consistent with the agreement and prevented disputes over ownership. As Jacob’s flock grew, the separation made the division of wealth increasingly obvious.

The mention of the ringstraked and brown animals “in the flock of Laban” may reflect the changes Laban made to the agreement over time. Jacob later complained that Laban had changed his wages ten times, sometimes declaring that the speckled would be Jacob’s, sometimes the ringstraked (31:7–8). Whatever terms Laban set, the flock produced accordingly. God would not let Laban’s shifting rules defeat His purpose. The God who sees did not need to correct each of Laban’s changes; He simply made the flock bear what the latest rule assigned to Jacob.

The verse depicts a man working hard within an unjust system. Jacob kept the agreement and separated his flocks honestly. God’s blessing rested on such faithfulness, not on the rods.

wordNotes.term: הִפְרִיד יַעֲקֹב (hifrid Yaʿaqov) — Jacob did separate
wordNotes.explanation: Parad in the hiphil means to divide or set apart. It is used of Abram and Lot parting their flocks and of nations being divided. Here Jacob separates his animals from Laban’s, keeping the agreement’s terms visible.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass, whensoever the stronger cattle did conceive, that Jacob laid the rods before the eyes of the cattle in the gutters, that they might conceive among the rods.” Jacob was selective. He used the rods only when the stronger animals were breeding, likely those that mated early in the season and produced healthier offspring.

This selection shows practical knowledge. Years of shepherding had taught Jacob which animals were vigorous. Choosing the stronger ones for breeding was sound husbandry. Yet his reliance on the rods shows that he still mixed observation with superstition, as believers often mingle real wisdom with misplaced trust. Like many in every generation, Jacob found it hard to separate what experience had taught him from what tradition had told him, and both were mixed in his practice.

The practice also raises a question of fairness. By ensuring that the stronger animals produced young that would be his, Jacob directed the best of the flock toward himself. Laban had cheated him repeatedly, and God later declared that He had seen Laban’s wrongs (31:12). God’s justice was at work, restoring to Jacob what had been withheld. Still, the narrative does not hold up Jacob’s cleverness as the model; it shows God bringing justice through a flawed servant.

wordNotes.term: הַמְקֻשָּׁרוֹת (hamqushsharot) — the stronger
wordNotes.explanation: The pual participle of qashar, “to bind,” describes animals that were firm, robust, or compact. It may refer to sturdy animals or those that bred early in the season. It contrasts with the “feeble” of verse 42.

verses.bibleText: But when the cattle were feeble, he put them not in: so the feebler were Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But when the cattle were feeble, he put them not in: so the feebler were Laban’s, and the stronger Jacob’s.” The result of Jacob’s selection was a divided flock: the robust animals became his, and the weaker remained Laban’s. Over six years the difference would accumulate dramatically. Jacob’s wealth was built on vigorous animals; Laban’s holdings gradually weakened.

There is a note of reversal in this outcome. Laban had given Jacob the weak-eyed Leah when he wanted Rachel, and he had removed the coloured animals to leave Jacob with nothing. Now the stronger stock passes to Jacob while Laban keeps the feeble. The schemer finds his own methods turned against him. Scripture often describes such reversals: “He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it” (Ecclesiastes 10:8). The bargain Laban had rigged to leave Jacob empty-handed became the measure by which Laban lost his best stock.

Yet the reader must hold two truths together. Jacob’s methods were not above reproach, and the narrator does not commend them. At the same time, God was acting justly toward a wronged servant. Jacob later told Laban that if the God of his fathers had not been with him, he would have been sent away empty (31:42). The real explanation of Jacob’s wealth lay not in strong or feeble cattle but in the presence of God.

Believers today are called to honest dealing even with dishonest people (Romans 12:17–21). Jacob’s story shows that God can defend His servants without their needing to match deceit with deceit.

wordNotes.term: הָעֲטֻפִים (haʿatufim) — the feebler
wordNotes.explanation: ʿAtaf means to be weak or faint, used elsewhere of a soul that faints. Here it describes the weaker animals that remained with Laban, contrasting with the stronger that became Jacob’s.

verses.bibleText: And the man increased exceedingly, and had much cattle, and maidservants, and menservants, and camels, and asses.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the man increased exceedingly, and had much cattle, and maidservants, and menservants, and camels, and asses.” The chapter ends with a summary of Jacob’s prosperity. The verb “increased” is the same one Jacob used of Laban’s growth in verse 30 and God used at Bethel when He promised that Jacob would spread abroad (28:14). Here it is intensified with “exceedingly,” literally “very, very.” Jacob, who arrived with only a staff, now possesses great wealth.

The list of possessions echoes the wealth of Abraham and Isaac (12:16; 24:35; 26:13–14). Flocks, servants, camels, and donkeys were the marks of a prosperous household. Jacob had traded the increase of his flocks for other goods, building a large estate. The God who blessed Abraham and Isaac was now blessing Jacob in the same way. Genesis takes care to show that each generation’s wealth came from the same faithful Giver.

The verse is the fulfilment of God’s promise at Bethel: “I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest” (28:15). Jacob had come to Haran fleeing, with nothing; God had given him wives, children, and wealth. Despite Laban’s fraud, Jacob’s own scheming, and the rivalry in his tents, God had kept His word. Chapter 31 makes the source plain: “God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me” (31:9).

This increase was not an end in itself. God was preparing Jacob to return to the land of promise, where his family would grow into a nation. The wealth gathered in Haran would sustain the household on the journey home. In the same way, the blessings God gives His people are meant to equip them for His purposes, not to settle them in a foreign land. The parallel with Israel leaving Egypt is not accidental: as Israel would go out with silver and gold after years of hard service (Exodus 12:35–36), so Jacob would go out from Laban with the wealth his labour had earned.

Jacob’s story points beyond itself to the greater Son of Israel. Jesus did not grow rich at another’s expense but became poor so that through His poverty many might be made rich (2 Corinthians 8:9). The truest wealth God gives is not cattle or servants but an inheritance that fades not away, reserved in heaven for those kept by His power (1 Peter 1:4–5).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּפְרֹץ הָאִישׁ מְאֹד מְאֹד (vayyifrots haʾish meʾod meʾod) — and the man increased exceedingly
wordNotes.explanation: Parats, “to break out,” is the verb of the Bethel promise and of Laban’s earlier growth. The doubled meʾod, “very very,” marks extraordinary increase. It shows the blessing that once flowed to Laban for Jacob’s sake now resting on Jacob himself.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What happens in a family when people try to win love and standing by outdoing one another?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God alone gives life and blessing; He works through a family torn by envy and scheming, hears the despised, and keeps His promise in spite of human expedients and injustice.
discussionQuestions: How do the names Rachel and Leah give their sons reveal what they believed about God and about each other?
Why does the narrator say that God hearkened to Leah and remembered Rachel instead of crediting the mandrakes?
In what ways does Jacob reap in Laban’s house what he had sown in Isaac’s house?
How does Genesis 31:9-12 change the way we read Jacob’s peeled rods?
What does Laban’s confession in verse 27 show about the difference between recognising God’s blessing and submitting to God?
commonMisunderstandings: The record of polygamy and concubinage describes what happened; it does not commend it, and its fruit in this family is jealousy and grief.
The mandrakes did not open Rachel’s womb; the text deliberately assigns every conception that matters to God.
Jacob’s rods were not a hidden law of nature or a model for success; the increase came from God’s blessing, as Jacob himself later confessed.
Leah’s and Rachel’s interpretations of their children’s births are their own words and are not always the narrator’s verdict.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the focus on God’s gracious faithfulness: He sees the unloved, remembers the barren, and protects the wronged worker, while the human rivalry around Him is told honestly as a warning.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Bring the empty place in your life to the God who hears, and stop trying to secure by rivalry or scheming what only He can give.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God is the Author of life and the faithful Keeper of His promises, whose grace carries sinful people toward His saving purpose fulfilled in Christ.
flow: Envy and rivalry leave both Rachel and Leah restless and unsatisfied.
Human expedients such as handmaids and mandrakes cannot supply what only God gives.
God hears the despised and remembers the barren in His own time.
Through this flawed family He forms the twelve tribes, from whom the promised Seed would come.
Christ, the true Son of Israel, gives the rest and acceptance these mothers sought in their children.
simpleIllustrations: Two people tugging on the same rope can both lose their grip; Rachel and Leah strained against each other while the gift came from Someone else entirely.
A farmer may plant and water, yet he never manufactures the life in the seed; Jacob could peel rods, but only God could make the flocks increase.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop striving to prove your worth and trust the God who remembers you and has given His Son for you?
cautions: Do not promise that every barren couple who prays will have children; God’s remembering takes many forms.
Do not use Jacob’s rods or Rachel’s mandrakes as patterns for faith or prosperity.
Speak gently about infertility, avoiding any suggestion that childlessness is a sign of God’s displeasure.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I envying someone else’s blessing instead of thanking God for what He has given me?
What “mandrakes” am I tempted to trust when I feel God is slow to act?
Do the names I give to my circumstances honour God or merely record my rivalry with others?
How can I serve faithfully under unfair treatment while leaving my vindication to God?
In what part of my life do I need to hear that God remembers me?
